newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel accuse each other, await Albright.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel accuse each other, await Albright.

text.p: Palestinians and Israelis traded accusations on Thursday as they waited for U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to decide whether to visit the Middle East to try to salvage peacemaking.
Albright has said she would make her maiden visit to the region at month's end if progress was made on the security issues.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross said before leaving the area on Wednesday that his success in getting Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials talking was a start in restoring security links.
His mission was spurred by a July 30 suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market that killed 16 people, including the attackers.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat charged on Thursday that Israel was not ready to work to save peacemaking.

"How can you dance the tango alone? You need a partner who is ready to dance with you. We say, 'Is this government really ready to work with us to preserve the peace process and protect it? Is it really ready to do so?' I am sorry to say the answer is no," Arafat said in the West Bank town of Ramallah.
Arafat, speaking to Israeli peace activists and left-wing lawmakers, condemned sanctions Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu imposed against Palestinians after the bombing.
"Netanyahu has to understand that patience has limits ...Instead of fighting terrorism he is fighting the Palestnian people," Arafat said.

Israel insists it will not lift a closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip or make financial transfers it owes the Palestinians until Arafat cracks down on militants. It denies Palestinians are suffering. Arafat says he has fought militants.
Israel has steadily lifted restrictions on Palestinian movements between towns in the West Bank but has insisted the main sanctions will remain firmly in place until Arafat acts.
On Thursday, the Israeli army said it had lifted its siege, or "internal closure", of Hebron and Ramallah but the town of Bethlehem and an area surrounding Jerusalem remained sealed off.
The cabinet secretary of Arafat's Palestinian Authority said the next move in the crisis was Washington's.
"The ball is now in the Americans' court," Cabinet Secretary Ahmed Abdel-Rahman told Reuters, saying that Israel was not seeking security cooperation but to dictate to Arafat.
Albright has said it was essential that Arafat made a "100 percent effort" to prevent militant attacks.
A senior U.S. official on Thursday told reporters he hoped Israel would make the financial transfers it owed the Palestinians once Arafat took action against militants.
"Measures that are taken that are punitive in nature ...holding up the money, is something that we think is not a good idea," he added, speaking on condition he not be named.
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan, speaking before Arafat's comments, said Israel had yet to see Arafat act.
"We don't see anything really concrete. We see a certain seriousness in their meetings with us and we welcome it. We are waiting to see if it translates into deeds," he told Reuters.

"We are not dictating anything. The fact is that agreements exist...The Palestinians must keep up their end of the bargain. And unless they do so, they will make a mockery of the agreements that we have signed and those that we intend to and want to sign in the future."
Albright's trip was expected to focus on reviving substantive negotiations frozen since Netanyahu broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
Israeli newspaper editorials and commentary were gloomy on peacemaking prospects.

Political analyst Shlomo Gazit wrote that the 1993 framework for Israel-PLO peacemaking reached in Oslo was dead and the sooner the sides acknowledged that, the sooner they could begin framing a new way of making a final peace.
"The Oslo agreement is dead," Gazit wrote in the Maariv daily, saying the core trust that was Oslo's lifeblood was gone.
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters Washington had to take charge of peacemaking.
"We simply have a zero trust level with Mr Netanyahu...which creates the need for a third party intervention," he said.
In Hebron, Palestinians said that a boy wounded in clashes with Israeli troops last month died in hospital. In the central West Bank, Israel partly demolished five Arab homes built without permits.
In Jerusalem, an Israeli court sentenced two border policemen to eight months in jail and 12 months suspended for brutalising Palestinians last October.
